title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models

paper.title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest.
Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored.
To fill this gap and better understand how text-to-image Transformers allocate and route attention, we explore this phenomenon of text-to-image transformers across bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive models.
Specifically, we explore whether attention sinks exist , where they emerge , and how they functionally influence generation .
Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns.
The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners.
Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads.
To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions.
It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores.
We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance.
Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Transformers have become a central architecture for modern generative modeling, but their attention maps often contain attention sinks , where a small set of token positions absorb disproportionately large attention mass [ 35 , 41 ] . Such phenomenon has been extensively studied in large language models (LLMs), where causal masking and sequence organization often cause early tokens to act as persistent attention anchors [ 41 , 32 , 13 , 14 ] . However, the prevailing understanding of attention sinks remains largely centered in LLMs, with limited exploration in other domains. Text-to-image Transformers differ substantially from LLMs. They jointly process text and image tokens, organize visual tokens according to spatial or multiscale structures, and generate images either through iterative diffusion denoising or autoregressive image-token prediction [ 9 , 21 , 3 , 34 , 15 ] . Therefore, their attention distributions might be relevant to modality boundaries, spatial topology, attention directionality, and generation stage. These properties may not be reflected by the conventional first-token sink of causal LLMs. Moreover, sink patterns reported in vision models [ 45 , 26 ] do not directly explain how attention is allocated during multimodal T2I generation. A systematic study of attention sinks in T2I models is thus needed not only to determine whether the phenomenon occurs beyond LLMs, but also to better understand how T2I Transformers allocate and route attention during generation. This paper addresses three fundamental questions: 1) whether attention sinks exist in modern T2I Transformers, 2) where they are located, and 3) are they functionally relevant to generation? To answer them, we conduct a systematic empirical study across three models: FLUX.1 and Z-Image as diffusion-based T2I Transformers, and Infinity-2B as an autoregressive T2I Transformer, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). We first characterize their attention distributions by sink strength, attention inequality, layer-head localization, positional preference, prompt sensitivity, and inference-time dynamics. Concretely, we evaluate these properties on GenEval [ 11 ] and DPG-Bench [ 17 ] , which cover diverse compositional generation and fine-grained text-image alignment. Then, we perform targeted interventions on attention routing, value contributions, sink-related heads, and candidate sink positions to assess their functional relevance. Finally, we introduce register tokens as dedicated non-semantic positions to examine whether sink-related attention can be redistributed without comprising synthesis quality. Our results show that attention-sink patterns are structured in both diffusion and autoregressive T2I transformers, yet their locations differ substantially across architectures. Autoregressive model exhibits pronounced concentration on the global first token, while the diffusion models concentrate attention near modality boundaries, within text-token regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, sink behavior is localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads and evolves across denoising or coarse-to-fine generation stages, suggesting that sink locations of T2I transformers are associated with the inference stage rather than fixed token positions. To investigate their influence on generation, we perform interventions on sink tokens, which reveal heterogeneous functional effects. Perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than the reported random or low-sink comparisons, indicating that certain sink-related heads participate in consequential generation pathways. In comparison, several sink-position perturbations have limited effects in bidirectional diffusion models. Additionally, register-token experiments further show that several configurations can redistribute attention while preserving or modestly improving generation performance. Together, these results extend the study of attention sinks beyond its language-centric formulation. Our analysis characterizes attention sinks as architecture-, stage-, and component-dependent phenomena and establishes an important distinction between where attention accumulates and where generation is functionally sensitive. Our contributions are summarized as: • We systematically explore and characterize attention sinks in bidirectional diffusion and causal autoregressive T2I Transformers across token positions, layers, heads, prompts, and generation stages. • We evaluate the functional relevance of sink-related components through targeted interventions and investigate register tokens as dedicated non-semantic positions for redistributing attention. • We provide an empirical foundation for controlled mechanistic analysis and for the principled design of attention mechanisms and token layouts in T2I Transformers.

sections.heading: 3 Analytical Framework
sections.text: We establish a unified framework for identifying, localizing, and intervening on attention sinks in T2I Transformers, with related metrics (Sec. 3.1 ), intervention strategies (Sec. 3.2 ), and experimental setup (Sec. 3.3 ).

This measures how generation changes when the output contribution of selected high-concentration heads is removed.

sections.heading: 3.3 Experimental Setups
sections.text: Models . We study two T2I Transformer paradigms: bidirectional denoising models, including FLUX.1-dev [ 21 ] and Z-Image [ 3 ] , and a causal autoregressive model, Infinity-2B [ 15 ] . During inference, all models generate × 1024 1024\!\times\!1024 images using their official inference settings. FLUX.1 and Z-Image use the EDM [ 20 ] sampler with 28 28 denoising steps, while Infinity-2B uses a bitwise sampler with a 13 13 -scale schedule. Token Layouts . Token layouts differ across models: Infinity follows a causal sequence, whereas FLUX.1 and Z-Image adopt a fixed interleaved structure. Moreover, FLUX.1 places text tokens first and Z-Image places image tokens first. We therefore define three positional relations: 1) sequence position, 2) text-side relation, and 3) image-side relation. In the following, token position refers to the index within the sequence, while modality relations are discussed separately. Datasets and Metrics . We evaluate on two complementary benchmarks: GenEval [ 11 ] , which contains 553 553 prompts for compositional generation such as counting, color attribution, and spatial relations, and DPG-Bench [ 17 ] , which contains 1065 1065 prompts for fine-grained text-image alignment. Together, they provide 1618 1618 prompts with distinct lengths and semantic densities. We report official GenEval and DPG-Bench scores for semantic alignment, and use HPSv2 [ 39 ] and ImageReward [ 42 ] as auxiliary preference and perceptual-quality metrics. For intervention tables, Δ ¯ \bar{\Delta} denotes the average percentage change across the reported metrics relative to the corresponding baseline. All evaluations follow the official protocols, and all experiments are conducted on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

sections.heading: 4.1 Effects of Token Position on Attention Sinks
sections.text: Attention sinks are positionally model-dependent . Fig. 1 (b) shows that Infinity-2B concentrates attention on its first and global token, whereas FLUX.1 places strong attention near structural text-image or layout positions. The aggregate statistics in Tab. 1 and Fig. 2 show the same pattern beyond the visual examples. The first position is rarely selected as a sink in the evaluated diffusion models with ρ 1 ​ ( 0 ) < 1 % \rho_{1}(0)\!<\!1\% , while Infinity-2B shows a pronounced position-0 concentration with ρ 1 ​ ( 0 ) = 37.52 % \rho_{1}(0)\!=\!37.52\% . Moreover, bidirectional diffusion models favor the text region and modality boundary, as the highlighted in the Fig. 2 . This shows that T2I attention sinks do not follow a universal first-token pattern inherited from language models. Instead, their preferred positions depend on the generation paradigm and token layout. Spatial corner bias in image tokens . The boundary and sink markers in Fig. 1 (b) motivate a closer look at image-layout positions. Fig. 2 shows prominent image-token peaks at FLUX.1 index 4544 4544 , the bottom-left corner, and Z-Image index 0 0 , the top-left corner of its image stream. These positions are not semantic but fixed layout anchors that repeatedly absorb attention. Infinity-2B’s analogous position is its sole 1 × 1 1\times 1 global-scale token, which represents a coarse global canvas rather than a local patch. Together, the visual examples and aggregate curves indicate that image-side sinks are tied to corners, boundaries, or global layout tokens. Takeaways: 1. Sink positions are model-dependent rather than universally tied to the first token. 2. Frequent sinks usually correspond to structural anchors, including global tokens, modality boundaries, and image-corner patches. sections.text: We use the sink concentration κ ( l , h ) \kappa^{(l,h)} to identify heads whose attention is dominated by a single key position. For simplicity, we denote head ( i , j ) (i,j) as L ​ i ​ H ​ j LiHj . Sink concentration is sparse across layers and heads . Fig. 3 shows that only about 3 % ∼ 5 % 3\%\sim 5\% of heads are sink-dominant in each model. Although their locations differ by models, this sparse localization is consistent across models. A larger count of sink‑dominant heads in a layer increases the likelihood of sink‑token emergence, while weaker sink‑head tendencies correspondingly mitigate the sink phenomenon. Sink placement occurs at model-specific depths . Sink depth follows each model’s behavior rather than a universal pattern. Takeaways: 1. Sink heads are sparsely localized in transformer. 2. Their locations differ across models rather than following a universal depth.

sections.heading: 4.4 Effects of Prompt on Attention Sinks
sections.text: We compare GenEval [ 11 ] and DPG-Bench [ 17 ] to examine whether attention sinks are stable under different prompt distributions. The layer-head concentration maps are highly correlated across the two datasets, with Pearson correlations above 0.98 for all three models, as shown in Tab. 3 . This indicates that the heads prone to sink behavior are largely stable under different prompt sets. Together with the pruning results in Tab. 6 , these results suggest that sink-head identity is more tied to model structure than to a specific prompt benchmark. sections.heading: 5.1 Impact of Intervention Strategies.
sections.text: We evaluate the three strategies from Sec. 3.2 using GenEval, DPG, HPSv2, and ImageReward. Fig. 1 (c) illustrates their intended targets, Fig. 1 (d) shows their visual effects, and Tab. 4 reports the aggregate scores. Across models, severity follows the intervention scope. Logit penalties produce the smallest average changes ( − 0.19 % -0.19\% , − 0.36 % -0.36\% , and − 2.79 % -2.79\% for FLUX.1, Z-Image, and Infinity-2B), indicating limited final-score sensitivity when only routing to the selected sinks is discouraged. Value substitution causes larger drops ( − 0.71 % -0.71\% , − 0.58 % -0.58\% , and − 5.45 % -5.45\% ), consistent with the selected sink values carrying useful generation information. Head pruning is most disruptive ( − 4.19 % -4.19\% , − 2.36 % -2.36\% , and − 6.56 % -6.56\% ), as it removes both sink routing and the surrounding head computation. Infinity-2B is consistently the most sensitive, which agrees with the first-token case in Fig. 1 (d). Sensitivity to sink token numbers . To test the effect of the perturbed sink-token count, we vary this number and plot Δ ¯ \bar{\Delta} under logit and value interventions in Fig. 5 . The slope is steepest for Infinity-2B, whose dominant sink coincides with the first/global token, while FLUX.1 and Z-Image degrade more gently, matching their more distributed sinks. This token-count ablation thus supports the positional analysis in Sec. 4.1 , as sink sensitivity grows with how much of the model-specific sink structure is covered. sections.heading: 6.1 Text-to-Image Transformer
sections.text: Transformer-based T2I generation has developed along two complementary paradigms: diffusion transformers and autoregressive models . Both of them rely heavily on multi-head attention as the core computational primitive. The seminal Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [ 27 ] first replaced the U-Net with a pure transformer architecture, building upon foundational diffusion frameworks [ 16 , 30 , 7 ] . SD3 [ 9 ] introduced the MMDiT, which employed joint self-attention for text and image modalities. This paradigm has since been advanced by open-source models such as FLUX.1 [ 21 ] , Z-Image [ 3 ] , Qwen-Image [ 37 , 47 ] , and Hunyuan-Image [ 4 ] , as well as commercial systems [ 1 , 10 , 12 ] . In contrast, autoregressive Transformers treat images as discrete token sequences and generate them left-to-right. Early works including DALL-E [ 28 ] , CogView [ 8 ] , and Parti [ 43 ] established the paradigm with large-scale transformer models. More recent efforts such as LlamaGen [ 33 ] revisited next-token prediction without visual inductive biases, VAR [ 34 ] introduced next-scale prediction for faster inference, and Infinity series [ 15 , 24 ] applied bit-wise quantization for efficient high-resolution generation. Despite these architectural differences, both paradigms exhibit structured attention behaviors, motivating our analysis.

sections.heading: 6.2 Attention Sinks in Transformers
sections.text: Attention sinks (AS) are tokens that absorb extremely high attention. This phenomenon arises from the sum-to-one constraint of Softmax: when no semantically relevant key exists, attention mass is forced onto specific uninformative tokens as a numerical no-op buffer [ 2 , 32 ] . AS were first characterized in autoregressive LLMs, where initial tokens dominate under causal masking [ 41 ] . Subsequent work empirically traces their emergence [ 13 , 14 , 31 ] , exploits them for context anchoring [ 25 ] , attention redistribution [ 36 , 44 ] , and connects them to activation outliers [ 32 ] . In Vision Transformers , Bondarenko et al. [2] show that sinks are localized on low‑information background patches, not on positional tokens. Darcet et al. [6] and Lappe and Giese [22] demonstrate that injecting learnable register tokens absorbs this excess attention. In Multimodal LLMs , visual sinks on non-semantic tokens degrade grounding [ 19 , 45 ] , and further studies examine visual information pathways [ 26 ] and audio-visual speech recognition [ 5 ] . Diffusion LMs exhibit distinct features compared to autoregressive counterparts. Rulli et al. [29] observe moving sinks that shift throughout the denoising process. Zhang et al. [46] further identify moving sinks as protecting against over‑mixing in diffusion while dynamic position hurts. In Diffusion Models , attention sinks have high norms [ 18 , 40 ] , while Wu and Summa [38] argue that they are not functional structures essential for semantic alignment. Li et al. [23] show that text template tokens act as implicit semantic registers. However, the extent to which findings transfer across diffusion and autoregressive T2I Transformers remains unclear. A unified comparison across layer, head, token-position, and generation-stage dimensions is still limited for recent text-to-image architectures.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: We presented a systematic study of attention sinks in text-to-image Transformers. Our results show that the evaluated T2I models do not all reproduce the canonical language-model first-token pattern, varying with multimodal token layouts and generation stages. The evaluated autoregressive model exhibits strong first-token attraction, whereas the evaluated bidirectional models concentrate sink mass near modality boundaries and spatial corner positions. Intervention experiments further show that model performance is sensitive to selected sink-related heads and positions, which motivates further study of dedicated non-semantic positions. Overall, attention sinks provide a useful lens for interpreting and potentially controlling generative attention in T2I models. Limitations and Future Work . Our study covers three text-to-image Transformers, leaving broader architectures, scales, and training recipes for future validation. We only focus on inference-time behavior, while understanding how attention sinks emerge during training remains an important next step.

Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored. To fill this gap and better understand how text-to-image Transformers allocate and route attention, we explore this phenomenon of text-to-image transformers across bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive models. Specifically, we explore whether attention sinks exist , where they emerge , and how they functionally influence generation . Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns. The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads. To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions. It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores. We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance. Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers. The evaluated diffusion models concentrate attention near modality boundaries and spatial corner positions, whereas Infinity-2B exhibits strong raw concentration at its first/global token. 1 Introduction Transformers have become a central architecture for modern generative modeling, but their attention maps often contain attention sinks , where a small set of token positions absorb disproportionately large attention mass [ 35 , 41 ] . Such phenomenon has been extensively studied in large language models (LLMs), where causal masking and sequence organization often cause early tokens to act as persistent attention anchors [ 41 , 32 , 13 , 14 ] . However, the prevailing understanding of attention sinks remains largely centered in LLMs, with limited exploration in other domains. Text-to-image Transformers differ substantially from LLMs. They jointly process text and image tokens, organize visual tokens according to spatial or multiscale structures, and generate images either through iterative diffusion denoising or autoregressive image-token prediction [ 9 , 21 , 3 , 34 , 15 ] . Therefore, their attention distributions might be relevant to modality boundaries, spatial topology, attention directionality, and generation stage. These properties may not be reflected by the conventional first-token sink of causal LLMs. Moreover, sink patterns reported in vision models [ 45 , 26 ] do not directly explain how attention is allocated during multimodal T2I generation. A systematic study of attention sinks in T2I models is thus needed not only to determine whether the phenomenon occurs beyond LLMs, but also to better understand how T2I Transformers allocate and route attention during generation. This paper addresses three fundamental questions: 1) whether attention sinks exist in modern T2I Transformers, 2) where they are located, and 3) are they functionally relevant to generation? To answer them, we conduct a systematic empirical study across three models: FLUX.1 and Z-Image as diffusion-based T2I Transformers, and Infinity-2B as an autoregressive T2I Transformer, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). We first characterize their attention distributions by sink strength, attention inequality, layer-head localization, positional preference, prompt sensitivity, and inference-time dynamics. Concretely, we evaluate these properties on GenEval [ 11 ] and DPG-Bench [ 17 ] , which cover diverse compositional generation and fine-grained text-image alignment. Then, we perform targeted interventions on attention routing, value contributions, sink-related heads, and candidate sink positions to assess their functional relevance. Finally, we introduce register tokens as dedicated non-semantic positions to examine whether sink-related attention can be redistributed without comprising synthesis quality. Our results show that attention-sink patterns are structured in both diffusion and autoregressive T2I transformers, yet their locations differ substantially across architectures. Autoregressive model exhibits pronounced concentration on the global first token, while the diffusion models concentrate attention near modality boundaries, within text-token regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, sink behavior is localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads and evolves across denoising or coarse-to-fine generation stages, suggesting that sink locations of T2I transformers are associated with the inference stage rather than fixed token positions. To investigate their influence on generation, we perform interventions on sink tokens, which reveal heterogeneous functional effects. Perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than the reported random or low-sink comparisons, indicating that certain sink-related heads participate in consequential generation pathways. In comparison, several sink-position perturbations have limited effects in bidirectional diffusion models. Additionally, register-token experiments further show that several configurations can redistribute attention while preserving or modestly improving generation performance. Together, these results extend the study of attention sinks beyond its language-centric formulation. Our analysis characterizes attention sinks as architecture-, stage-, and component-dependent phenomena and establishes an important distinction between where attention accumulates and where generation is functionally sensitive. Our contributions are summarized as: • We systematically explore and characterize attention sinks in bidirectional diffusion and causal autoregressive T2I Transformers across token positions, layers, heads, prompts, and generation stages. • We evaluate the functional relevance of sink-related components through targeted interventions and investigate register tokens as dedicated non-semantic positions for redistributing attention. • We provide an empirical foundation for controlled mechanistic analysis and for the principled design of attention mechanisms and token layouts in T2I Transformers. 2 Preliminaries Attention Sinks . Both of them rely heavily on multi-head attention as the core computational primitive. The seminal Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [ 27 ] first replaced the U-Net with a pure transformer architecture, building upon foundational diffusion frameworks [ 16 , 30 , 7 ] . SD3 [ 9 ] introduced the MMDiT, which employed joint self-attention for text and image modalities. This paradigm has since been advanced by open-source models such as FLUX.1 [ 21 ] , Z-Image [ 3 ] , Qwen-Image [ 37 , 47 ] , and Hunyuan-Image [ 4 ] , as well as commercial systems [ 1 , 10 , 12 ] . In contrast, autoregressive Transformers treat images as discrete token sequences and generate them left-to-right. Early works including DALL-E [ 28 ] , CogView [ 8 ] , and Parti [ 43 ] established the paradigm with large-scale transformer models. More recent efforts such as LlamaGen [ 33 ] revisited next-token prediction without visual inductive biases, VAR [ 34 ] introduced next-scale prediction for faster inference, and Infinity series [ 15 , 24 ] applied bit-wise quantization for efficient high-resolution generation. Despite these architectural differences, both paradigms exhibit structured attention behaviors, motivating our analysis. 6.2 Attention Sinks in Transformers Attention sinks (AS) are tokens that absorb extremely high attention. This phenomenon arises from the sum-to-one constraint of Softmax: when no semantically relevant key exists, attention mass is forced onto specific uninformative tokens as a numerical no-op buffer [ 2 , 32 ] . AS were first characterized in autoregressive LLMs, where initial tokens dominate under causal masking [ 41 ] . Subsequent work empirically traces their emergence [ 13 , 14 , 31 ] , exploits them for context anchoring [ 25 ] , attention redistribution [ 36 , 44 ] , and connects them to activation outliers [ 32 ] . In Vision Transformers , Bondarenko et al. [2] show that sinks are localized on low‑information background patches, not on positional tokens. Darcet et al. [6] and Lappe and Giese [22] demonstrate that injecting learnable register tokens absorbs this excess attention. A unified comparison across layer, head, token-position, and generation-stage dimensions is still limited for recent text-to-image architectures. 7 Conclusions We presented a systematic study of attention sinks in text-to-image Transformers. Our results show that the evaluated T2I models do not all reproduce the canonical language-model first-token pattern, varying with multimodal token layouts and generation stages. The evaluated autoregressive model exhibits strong first-token attraction, whereas the evaluated bidirectional models concentrate sink mass near modality boundaries and spatial corner positions. Intervention experiments further show that model performance is sensitive to selected sink-related heads and positions, which motivates further study of dedicated non-semantic positions. Overall, attention sinks provide a useful lens for interpreting and potentially controlling generative attention in T2I models. Limitations and Future Work .
